reactions.name: lipid A -> modified lipid A
reactions.evidence: pmrCAB operon, activating the response regulator PmrA which induces transcription of genes encoding enzymes that covalently modify lipid A and core sugar phosphates with aminoarabinose (Ara4N) and phosphoethanolamine (pEtN), • mutation of PhoQ leads to a change in the structure and inflammatory properties of the lipid A part of LPS, • associated with bacterial adaptation in the respiratory tract of patients with cystic fibrosis. [ 44 ] [ 81 ] Salmonella Typhimurium Enteroinvasive bacterial pathogen that usually occurs after ingestion of contaminated food or water. S. Typhimurium causes self-limiting gastroenteritis in humans and typhoid-like fever in mice. It forms biofilms on abiotic surfaces such as plastic and egg conveyor belts, which may play a role in the survival of this organism in the environment. S. Typhimurium also grows in exopolysaccharide-rich biofilms on the surface of gallstones, which may contribute to ineffective antibiotic treatment and facilitate typhoid transmission. The biofilm shed from colonised gallstones is likely to be the source of recurrent infections. • regulates LPS modification loci (e.g. pbgP and ugd ), • activates TCS BasSR, which is responsible for LPS synthesis and modification of lipid A to increase colistin resistance, • regulates lipid components of the OM including LPS and glycerolphospholipids, • is indirectly involved in the regulation of colistin resistance, • is involved in antimicrobial peptide resistance, • regulates the expression of genes essential for intracellular survival, partly through the activation of the type III secretion system of the pathogenicity island, • plays an important role in defending bacteria against NO compounds produced in the innate response, while also becoming a target for reactive nitrogen species produced by activated phagocytes, • responds to acidic pH possibly enabling virulence of the bacteria in the host. [ 46 ] [ 81 ] [ 82 ] [ 83 ] [ 84 ][ 85 ] Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis S. Enteritidis is the most common foodborne bacterium (salmonellosis) associated with the consumption of egg products and undercooked poultry. • is involved in resistance to quinolones and cephalosporins. [ 81 ] [ 86 ] Klebsiella pneumoniae It has been recognised as an urgent threat to human health due to its extremely drug-resistant strains. Numerous studies address the molecular mechanisms underlying antibiotic resistance in K. pneumoniae , while others analyse the virulence strategies of this pathogen. • activation of transcription of the arn operon, via a TCS RR, • action in response to low magnesium concentrations. [ 87 ] [ 88 ] [ 89 ] Escherichia coli E. coli belongs to the Enterobacteriaceae family. It is the most widespread inhabitant of the digestive tract of humans and warm-blooded animals and is one of the most important pathogens. It is responsible for a wide spectrum of diseases. They have been recognised as agents of food-borne enteritis. They owe their pathogenicity, among other things, to their ability to grow under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions. • system in the bacterium is involved in modifications of the LPS core region, which affects resistance to tetracycline and glycylcycline antibiotics. [ 10 ] [ 90 ] [ 91 ] [ 92 ] Shigella A facultative intracellular Gram-negative pathogen that causes shigellosis by penetrating and replicating in human colonic epithelial cells. This invasive process causes ulcerative lesions that result in bloody and purulent diarrhoea characteristic of bacterial dysentery. The bacteria are transmitted by the faecal–oral route and attack the mucosa of the colon. Shigella is highly infectious and causes shigellosis by infecting as few as 10–100 organisms. • acts as a virulence regulator, as it participates in the regulation of lower genes responsible for virulence factors in bacteria, • functions in response to extracellular Mg 2+ signals, pH and antimicrobial peptides. [ 9 ] [ 78 ] Yersinia pestis Gram-negative pathogenic bacterium characterised by virulence factors such as an OM protein or iron uptake system. Y. pestis uses these to attack the human immune system, allowing the bacteria to replicate unrestrictedly in the lymph nodes and lungs, causing plague. • shows sensitivity to oxidative stress, • shows sensitivity to low pH. [ 93 ] [ 94 ] Stenotrophomonas maltophilia S. maltophilia is a global, environmental Gram-negative multidrug-resistant strain pathogen that is most commonly associated with human respiratory infections. It is an important nosocomial pathogen. Mortality rates for this pathogen range from 14 to 69% in patients with bacteraemia. • is involved in resistance to β-lactams, because PhoPQ weakened the induced β-lactamase activity. [ 95 ] [ 96 ] Erwinia chrysanthemi This bacterium is a member of the Enterobacteriaceae family. The pathogenic behaviour is characterised by rapid necrosis of parenchymatous tissues and symptoms of soft rot, caused mainly by pectic enzymes that degrade the central lamellae and primary cell wall in plants. • shows sensitivity to environmental magnesium limitation and is involved in iron metabolism.
